title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service elementary science teachers integrated ChatGPT into lesson planning, with a particular focus on distinguishing feasible, appropriate uses of generative AI from inappropriate or overextended uses. The authors frame the study against a broader debate in AI-in-education research: much of the literature is visionary or theoretical, while empirical evidence about how ChatGPT can actually be used in classroom-facing instructional design remains limited.

The study involved 29 pre-service elementary teachers enrolled at a Korean teachers’ university. After four 2-hour instructional sessions introducing ChatGPT, discussing its educational possibilities, and reviewing science teaching methods and lesson-plan construction, participants drafted a 45-minute elementary science lesson plan that incorporated ChatGPT and attached a simulated chat example. The lesson plans were evaluated with a modified TPACK-based rubric (TIAR), and participants also answered open-ended survey questions about why they chose certain content/methods, why ChatGPT seemed useful, and what outcomes they expected.

Findings were largely descriptive and exploratory rather than causal. Participants integrated ChatGPT across multiple science domains and many instructional strategies, most often cooperative learning, POE, and the learning cycle. Overall lesson-plan quality was moderately high, but teachers were weaker at selecting the most appropriate ChatGPT functions than at aligning ChatGPT with content goals or instructional strategies. Qualitative responses suggested that pre-service teachers saw ChatGPT as useful for questioning, individualized support, and formative feedback, while also worrying about inaccuracy and student over-dependence. The paper concludes that pre-service teachers can envision many pedagogical uses of ChatGPT, but that more empirical research, especially in real classrooms and with causal designs, is needed before strong claims about instructional impact can be made.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive qualitative/descriptive study with a small preservice sample (n=29) and no randomized or comparison-based causal test of outcomes. It provides useful empirical evidence about lesson-plan integration, but it does not establish student-level impact.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but indirect and modest evidence of how ChatGPT might be integrated in K-12 science lesson planning, rather than measured effects on learners. Because outcomes are largely perceived or rubric-based design quality, generalizable impact is unclear.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used in pre-service elementary science teachers' lesson-plan generation and simulated classroom questioning for science lessons, including generating supporting information, role-play scripts, adaptive follow-up questions, and formative feedback within lesson plans.

finding.finding_summary: This is a descriptive, preservice-adjacent study rather than a causal test of student learning. Across 29 pre-service teachers' lesson plans, ChatGPT was proposed for scientific inquiry supports such as prediction, explanation, exploration, and formative assessment, and the plans averaged M=3.29/4 on a modified TPACK-based rubric (SD=.91).
finding.measure: Modified TPACK-based lesson-plan rubric (TIAR-derived scores) and qualitative analysis of lesson plans/survey responses

finding.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers expected ChatGPT to support critical thinking, self-directed learning, and collaborative learning when embedded in structured science lessons. These are perception-based findings from lesson plans and open-ended survey responses (n=29), not direct measures of student outcomes.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses and lesson-plan coding for anticipated uses such as critical thinking, self-directed learning, and cooperation

finding.finding_summary: Participants anticipated that ChatGPT could increase student motivation and interest through individualized support and instant questioning, but they also worried about over-dependence and misinformation. The study reports perceptions and design judgments only; no student affect outcomes were experimentally measured.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses on anticipated motivation, interest, and concerns about dependence

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was described as useful for lesson planning, organizing role-play activities, summarizing student-generated scenarios, and providing additional information or feedback, suggesting perceived efficiency gains for teachers. The study's quantitative result for lesson-plan quality was M=3.29/4 (SD=.91), with stronger scores for instructional strategies & ChatGPT (M=3.48, SD=.99) than for function selection (M=3.00, SD=.93).
finding.measure: Lesson-plan rubric scores and qualitative descriptions of planning support/feedback functions
